title: Colorado small town abandoned after all elected officials resign, water concerns grow
description: Hartman, Colorado, a town of 30 residents, was declared abandoned after all elected officials resigned and its water system became a health hazard.
fullText:
A small town in Colorado has been declared abandoned by the state after its remaining elected officials resigned, leading its troubled water system to become a "health hazard" to its residents, according to state officials.

The Office of the Colorado Secretary of State said the determination was made this week after a public hearing showed that "the Town of Hartman had no Board of Trustees or Town Clerk, was unable to hold a town election, and owned infrastructure critical for the treatment or delivery of water to residents."

"Importantly, not determining that the Town of Hartman is abandoned as contemplated by § 31-3-201(1)(b), C.R.S. (2026), would leave the residents in further legal limbo during a health hazard, with no authority to conduct business, hold elections, or fix their water infrastructure so that clean water can be delivered to the town residents," Deputy Secretary of State Andrew Kline wrote in an abandonment order. "Abandonment is the only legal mechanism in Colorado statute that creates an avenue for residents of the area to receive clean water."

Disneyland Guests Left Scrambling After Water Outage Shuts Bathrooms And Restaurants

Hartman, which has a population of 30 in southeast Colorado, saw its three active trustees resign in January, a day after a brawl erupted between four women following a board of trustees meeting, according to The Denver Post.

"Our safety was more important than having a government," Pam Packer, one of the trustees who resigned, told the newspaper, which also reported that the mayor resigned in October and that Hartman previously was grappling with embezzlement allegations and restraining orders.

Kline said in the abandonment order that in mid-June, "Ms. Jessie Simmons, a self-attested resident, landowner, and elector of the Town of Hartman, submitted a written application to the Secretary of State for determination of abandonment for the Town of Hartman alleging that the town does not have a board of trustees or town clerk, is unable to hold an election, and owns and operates water infrastructure needed to treat and deliver water to residents."

"Ms. Simmons further asserted that as of time of her application, the Town of Hartman had lacked chlorine in its water for over one month and the water was not potable and 'smells horrible.' She stated that the Town of Hartman had been under an order to boil water for months," he wrote.

Experts Reveal How To Avoid Deadly Legionnaires' Disease As Nyc Outbreak Kills 5

At a hearing on July 13, Eric Bergman, the director of the Division of Local Government for the Department of Local Affairs, "testified that he has regional managers throughout the state, and one in Southeast Colorado that has worked extensively with the Town of Hartman for the last 5 or 6 years," according to Kline.

"Mr. Bergman also testified that since 2022, DOLA representatives have been in the Town of Hartman over 30 times helping with elections, turnover, recalls, resignations, budgets, audits, grant administration, and training of new officials. In January of 2026, DOLA received letters of resignation from each of the town's then-Trustees. Since the resignation of these elected officials, no government officials or government remain in the Town of Hartman," the order stated.

"There are no government officials in the Town of Hartman who are authorized to approve contracts, spend funds, appoint replacements, certify elections, or make decisions regarding the Town of Hartman's water system. Mr. Bergman testified there is also no clerk or governing body to call, conduct, or certify a municipal election," it continued.

"According to Mr. Bergman, the Town of Hartman is facing a public health threat. Mr. Bergman testified that the Town of Hartman has been on a boil advisory since last October 2025, and the water currently needs testing and chlorine. The water tank is compromised and needs repair or replacement," Kline also wrote in the order. "There is no one operating the water system at this time. DOLA, along with the Colorado Department of Health and Environment had previously provided grants for more than $1 million to the Town of Hartman to work on the water system. Those funds were reimbursement-based. However, without government officials, the Town is unable to enter any contracts that would enable it to access the grant funds."

The Office of Colorado's Secretary of State said that, following the abandonment order, "All existing streets, avenues, and alleys previously located within the abandoned town that are not owned by a third party shall be vested in the Board of County Commissioners of Prowers County," and that "Ownership of water infrastructure critical for the treatment or delivery of water to residents shall be vested in Prowers County, which shall transfer said infrastructure to an entity whose primary purpose is water treatment or delivery."

title: Kennedy to host cooking show with focus on inexpensive meals
description: Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has launched a show geared toward teaching Americans how to cook healthy, inexpensive meals. “Thanks to President Trump, we flipped the ...
fullText:
Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has launched a show geared toward teaching Americans how to cook healthy, inexpensive meals.

"Thanks to President Trump, we flipped the food pyramid and put real food back where it belongs: at the center of the American plate," Kennedy said in a video he posted Wednesday to YouTube touting "The Real Food Show."

"I'm traveling across America, connecting with renowned chefs to show families how to cook delicious, nutritious meals with real ingredients, and all at affordable prices," the HHS secretary added. "America, it's time to eat real food. Let's get cooking."

The show's first episode aired Thursday on YouTube, with Kennedy and celebrity chef Andrew Gruel teaming up to prepare crispy salmon cakes with apple, white beans and green salad.

In January, Kennedy unveiled new dietary guidelines for Americans, placing vegetables, fruits, proteins, dairy and healthy fats at the top of the food pyramid and whole grains at the bottom.

The guidelines also called on Americans to avoid "highly processed foods" and refined carbohydrates. The move was part of Kennedy's efforts to address the root causes of chronic disease.

"Diets rich in vegetables and fruits reduce disease risk more effectively than many drugs," Kennedy said at a White House press briefing outlining the changes. "All grains outperform refined carbohydrates."

"Added sugars, especially sugar-sweetened beverages, drive metabolic disease, and today, our government declares war on added sugar, highly processed foods loaded with additives, added sugar and excess salt."

To lower levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, known as "bad" cholesterol, the Mayo Clinic recommends eating fiber-rich foods such as oats, beans and apples; filling your plate with fruits and vegetables; and eating whole grains instead of refined grains.

Kennedy told USA Today his new cooking show aims to convince Americans that eating healthier does not cost more.

The price of food at home and away from home both rose by 0.2 percent from May to June, according to the consumer price index, a popular measure of inflation.

"When we published the dietary guidelines, there was immediately sort of a good reaction, but also a little trepidation from the public and from critics saying that this food is a lot more expensive than the ultraprocessed food that we've been eating," Kennedy told USA Today. "And that's not true."

title: Delta-8, THC products come off Texas shelves Friday under new state ban
description: Starting Friday, Texas health officials are reclassifying Delta-8, Delta-10 and other THC isomers as controlled substances. Here's what to know.
fullText:
The deadline for various Delta-8 and THC products is here, as the products will be leaving shelves in Texas on Friday.

Starting July 31, the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) is set to reclassify Delta-8 THC and several other hemp-derived THC isomers — that are not delta-9 THC — as controlled substances in the state.

DSHS adopted new definitions for "Tetrahydrocannabinols" (THC) and "Marihuana Extract," with the change affecting products containing cannabinoids such as Delta-8, Delta-10, Delta-, and THCP, which was published in a July 10 public notice in the Texas Register.

In a July 27 social media post, the Texas Hemp Business Council said businesses cannot sell these products after July 31 and advised them to evaluate their inventory and prepare to remove or sell through products containing more than trace amounts of cannabinoids that fall within the reinstated definition.

Short answer: no under state and federal law.

However, Texas does allow medical use of low-THC cannabis through the state's Compassionate Use Program.

Products like delta-8 and THCA flower can create effects strikingly similar to those of delta-9 THC — the main intoxicating compound in cannabis, often called weed — which is illegal in Texas.

The key difference is how they're made and how they behave.

Delta-8 is a modified form of THC found in small amounts in hemp and usually converted from other cannabinoids. It can produce intoxicating or psychoactive effects, but it is not the same compound as Delta-9 THC.

THCA is sold as raw hemp flower and isn't intoxicating on its own.

But when it's heated — like by smoking or vaping — it turns into delta-9 THC, the same compound found in cannabis.

Mateo Rosiles is the Texas Connect reporter for USA TODAY and its regional papers in Texas. Got a news tip for him? Email him at mrosiles@usatodayco.com.

title: Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband details ‘big spiral’ as expert says one part ‘scared me’ in mom’s murder trial
description: Patrick Clancy testified about his ex-wife's mental health spiral on Seroquel and her intrusive thoughts about harming their children before the killings.
fullText:
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Patrick Clancy, the father of three young children strangled inside their Massachusetts home, became the first witness Monday in his ex-wife's murder trial, offering jurors a harrowing account of the mental health decline he witnessed before their deaths.

He was the first witness called in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, who faces murder charges in the deaths of the couple's three children in January 2023. Prosecutors argue she acted deliberately, while defense attorneys contend severe mental illness drove her actions.

Patrick described watching his then-wife fall into a "big spiral" after she began taking Seroquel, testifying that she lost weight, became severely depressed and began expressing suicidal thoughts.

"Awful," he said when asked how Lindsay was doing physically after starting the medication. "That was really where her big spiral started. She started to lose a lot of weight, and she became very depressed, and she was having a really hard time."

Lindsay Clancy's Husband Could Testify For Her At Trial Over Deaths Of Their Three Children

Patrick also testified that Lindsay told him she was experiencing intrusive thoughts about harming their children, although she denied having a plan and said the thoughts disturbed her.

"I never saw Lindsay harm the kids," he told jurors.

Margaret McLean, a former criminal prosecutor and trial attorney who teaches law at Boston College's Carroll School of Management, said Patrick's measured delivery did little to conceal the anguish of a father being forced to retrace the months preceding his children's deaths.

"I think his demeanor on the stand is really quite clinical. He's telling it as it is," McLean told Fox News Digital. "You can see the anguish within this man's eyes, his facial expressions. You can tell he's anguished up there, and it's a horrible thing to have to relive and talk about."

McLean said Patrick appeared to be compartmentalizing his emotions as he listened carefully to the questions and provided straightforward answers.

"He's got to get through this," she said. "He's got to listen to the questions and provide the answers as best he can, and I think that he's doing that."

Heated Lindsay Clancy Courtroom Exchange Over 911 Call, Crime Scene Photos Sets Stage For Mom's Murder Trial

Patrick testified that he was not concerned for the children's safety when Lindsay first shared that the intrusive thoughts were telling her to hurt herself as well as her children. Moments after discussing the thoughts, he said, she could be seen making the children lunch, playing with them or preparing them for bed.

Patrick told jurors that he became alarmed after Lindsay was prescribed 13 psychiatric medications in the months prior to the murders and that he pushed for an in-person appointment because he believed there was a "disconnect" between the seriousness of her condition and the brief telehealth sessions she was receiving.

"It seemed like most of her telehealth appointments were pretty quick, and there just wasn't, like, a lot of attention," he said.

Patrick also described taking Lindsay to hospital emergency departments and helping her enter McLean Hospital after she continued expressing suicidal thoughts.

He testified that he "would have paid anything" if insurance had become an obstacle to keeping her hospitalized.

The testimony could leave jurors asking whether the warning prompted an adequate response, McLean said, while cautioning against placing blame on Patrick or family members who may not have understood the severity of the risk.

"So many people don't understand mental health today, so I'm not blaming him at all," McLean said. "Anybody might have done what he did, but that's the part that scared me."

WATCH: Lindsay Clancy clutches tissues as jurors hear about her three children

Patrick's testimony followed starkly different opening statements from prosecutors and the defense.

Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham told jurors that Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were "deliberately and meticulously killed" by their mother on Jan. 24, 2023.

Buckingham alleged that Clancy deliberately sent Patrick from their Duxbury home to pick up medication and takeout food, giving herself enough time to strangle each child with an exercise band before attempting to kill herself.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

McLean said Buckingham gave jurors a "roadmap of cold, calculated intent" while humanizing each child's interests and focusing on the time and physical effort required to carry out three separate strangulations.

"The prosecution did that because she [Buckingham] wants the jury to remember that the act of strangulation takes time and physical effort," McLean said. "It requires a conscious choice to continue three separate times."

The Commonwealth's strategy, she said, is to reject the defense's bid that Clancy suffered a sudden psychotic break and instead portray her as organized, purposeful and controlled.

During opening statements, defense attorney Kevin Reddington conceded that Clancy killed the children but argued that the only meaningful dispute is what was happening inside her mind.

"She knows that she killed these children," Reddington told jurors. "The issue for consideration is what was going on in that woman's mind."

McLean described the concession as a calculated move by a veteran trial attorney.

"By doing that, he is attempting to strip the prosecution of their shock value and force the jury to look purely at Lindsay Clancy's mental capacity," she said.

Reddington argued that Clancy had no motive to kill children she had loved and nurtured. He also displayed graphic hospital photographs showing Clancy with injuries to her neck and wrists.

McLean said the defense was framing Clancy's paralysis "not as a consequence of a crime, but as the tragic final symptom of a complete postpartum psychotic break."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, has pleaded not guilty to three counts each of murder and strangulation. Her attorneys do not dispute that she killed the children but argue that she lacked criminal responsibility because of severe postpartum psychosis.

Judge William Sullivan told jurors that the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible when the children were killed.

"It's going to be black and white for some people, gray area for other people," McLean said. "It is going to be one of the hardest things that this jury, or any jury, will ever have to decide."

title: Mitch McConnell's office releases new photo of senator amid health questions
description: The 84-year-old lawmaker was first hospitalized on June 14 after a fall and subsequently treated for pneumonia.
fullText:
WASHINGTON – Six weeks after he was hospitalized for a fall and pneumonia, Sen. Mitch McConnell's doctors still have not medically cleared him to return to work or leave a rehabilitation facility, the Capitol physician's office said.

Since June, the Kentucky Republican's health has been a source of widespread speculation and interest. He has missed 38 roll call votes in the Senate, including on key measures such as the annual defense policy bill and ending the Iran war, as well as high-profile confirmation hearings for crucial Trump nominees like Todd Blanche, who is awaiting a vote to become the next attorney general.

All summer his office has provided only limited updates on his condition. But in a statement July 27, McConnell, 84, said he was still having "intense physical therapy" and wouldn't be able to travel to western Kentucky for the annual Fancy Farm picnic, a marquee political event in the state.

"As always, I appreciate all of your continued well wishes, and I'm looking forward to getting back to the Senate and to Kentucky soon," he said.

The Office of the Attending Physician, which provides medical services and guidance to members of Congress, said the lifelong effects of McConnell's bout with childhood polio continue to be a "significant factor in his mobility." Doctors visit with him every day.

"Since his discharge from hospital care, he has maintained a strenuous course of physical therapy and rehabilitation, including multiple sessions a day designed to rebuild strength and reduce the risk of future falls," the office said in a statement.

McConnell also released a new photo, dated July 26, of himself alongside his wife, Elaine Chao. Though his Senate colleagues say they've talked to him several times by phone over the course of his absence, the former majority leader hasn't spoken publicly since his departure. He also hasn't given any external interviews.

His office did not provide a tentative date for when he could be expected back at work in the Senate, which is scheduled to depart for a monthlong recess in two weeks on Aug. 7.

title: Cycling in rude health thanks to awesome Pogacar and stringent testing
description: Tour de France fans were spoilt for choice in Paris when it came to drinking in the drama of cycling's greatest race.
fullText:
Tour de France fans were spoilt for choice in Paris when it came to drinking in the drama of cycling's greatest race.

Should their attention be all on Tadej's Pogacar's crowning as the joint most successful rider of all time, with five Tour titles?

But then what about Mathieu van der Poel's superhero-style victory on the final stage, climaxing magnificently on the Champs-Elysees?

Or would the focus be on the sheer passion of a huge, fervent crowd which lined the streets on Montmartre and around Sacre-Coeur?

That last element illustrated a sport in rude health and again raised the question of why organisers had not run the traditional closing stage over the scenic cobbled hill before its debut visit last year.

Pogacar, the rarely beaten 27-year-old Slovenian, is widely regarded now as cycling's greatest of all time.

The fifth Tour win helps in that respect, matching fellow greats Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain – but Pogacar can also point to his many successes elsewhere in cycling's other huge events, such as one-day monuments.

Brutal Belgian Merckx stood alone as the sport's greatest before now, thanks to a similar versatility on the bike – capable, like Pogacar, of winning in all formats: time trials, cobbles, high mountains and even some sprints.

But perhaps what elevates Pogacar to the top now is his respectful demeanour, paying tribute as he did in Paris to every one of his domestiques by name, before thanking his family.

He also shepherded his young UAE-Team Emirates-XRG team-mate Isaac del Toro across the line on more than one occasion during this year's race when his own job was done.

The fact Pogacar achieved what he did while most of his team-mates - and possibly even himself - suffered sickness across the second half of the Tour is even more remarkable.

The Tour de France still is, after all, one of the hardest events in elite sport.

The Tour de France has a chequered history that cannot be forgotten.

"He knows what the record is," Lance Armstrong said on social media following Sunday's result, referring to Pogacar.

The American's record of seven Tour de France victories between 1999 and 2005 has long since been wiped from the record books following the revelation of his systematic doping.

And those in the sport have fairly diligently avoided mentioning his name since.

But the night-time anti-doping tests during this year's Tour, which the International Testing Agency (ITA) told BBC Sport were undertaken as an "exceptional operation" and because time was of the essence, once again raised questions in a sport which doesn't need them, thanks to that dark past.

Testing at such anti-social hours is rare and requires additional permission, and some suspect it may have been a factor in Jonas Vingegaard's Tour-ending crash after he was woken at 2am the previous night, and Pogacar himself at 5am.

Others were tested at night, too, and all riders were tested during the race. But what were the ITA looking for?

They wouldn't say, specifically, but one possible explanation for night-time testing of professional cyclists appears to be to gather as much information as possible to try to understand micro-dosing. That is where an athlete could take performance-enhancing drugs, such as red blood cell stimulant EPO or anabolic steroids, in very small quantities to evade detection on the Athlete Biological Passport, which is endorsed by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) and used across cycling.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing in the case of Pogacar, Vingegaard or any of those tested at night this year.

Past findings produced by Wada suggest micro-dosing could evade detection methods, and so the scope to cheat in professional sport remains, meaning all efforts must be taken to ensure nobody beats the system.

The ITA cannot confirm when the results of the Tour tests will be made public, but EF Education-Easypost boss Jonathan Vaughters told BBC Sport: "Doubts? Actually [those tests] solve my doubts."

Vaughters, who doped during his riding career, is now reformed.

He said during this year's race: "If we had 24-hour testing in 2001 when EPO tests were first introduced we would have had a huge number of riders excluded from the sport, including me. And it would have saved 25 years of drama.

"So I mean we wouldn't have had to go through Lance Armstrong... The problem would have been solved immediately in 2000.

"If you introduce a low enough dose of a peptide hormone, the clearance time can be four hours - if you take it at 11 it'll be out of the system at 3am, so it makes a difference. The testing technology is evolving quickly.

"If you want to watch a clean sport, watch cycling, most other sports' testing is a complete joke.

"Why is cycling so hyper-focused? History. This is human F1 car racing; this is edge of human performance; boundaries are always going to be pushed."

Many riders and team bosses won't go near the 'D' word, and the consensus is 'believe what you are seeing' when Pogacar accelerates away and wins by, at times, a matter of minutes, and when others perform their own remarkable feats in the saddle.

Huge numbers of people do believe what they see.

About 500,000 spectators turned out in Paris on Sunday, with 180,000 around Montmartre alone.

And it doesn't stop at the Tour de France, as many of the bigger races on the calendar are seeing notably bigger numbers.

"You can't get to certain parts to watch it any more, everyone has been there all day. Especially this year," said one journalist at Paris-Roubaix in April.

"There's so much traffic and so many people."

And many fans have noticed the increase in numbers.

Another 500,000 people were estimated to have lined the roads up to Alpe d'Huez last Friday, as videos emerged on social media of crowds setting up camp days before, drinking and partying prior to the race arriving.

At the end of Friday's stage, Movistar's Colombian climber Einer Rubio was even involved in a harrowing incident when he crashed, face-first, into the back of one of the service cars belonging to Pogacar's team, breaking the glass.

The car had been forced to stop abruptly when a spectator fell immediately into its path.

Rubio was forced to abandon the race after being given 20 stitches in hospital.

The presence of Britain's women's Tour winner Lizzie Deignan and record Tour stage win holder Mark Cavendish on the Champs-Elysees on Sunday was a timely reminder that Britain will hosts six stages of the men's and women's Tour de France races next summer.

It will be summer when British fans hope Netcompany Ineos Cycling's new injection of investment will pay dividends – after they failed to win a stage in this year's race – and riders such as Tom Pidcock can light up the race on home soil.

Some 30.2m people cycled at least once in Britain in the past year, according to British Cycling, which is the highest number it has been since 2019-20.

While Pogacar will probably prevent it happening in 2027, many thousands of Britons are still expected to flock to witness the race in motion.

fullText:
The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. We need to develop systems to strengthen public health as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design

As artificial intelligence rapidly transforms the biological sciences, it is pushing the future of biology in two opposing directions. AI can help bad actors generate recipes for biological weapons with just a few keystrokes and computational prompts. At the same time, AI can track disease outbreaks and deliver critical public health information to millions of people in real time – potentially stopping a deadly outbreak in its tracks. What we are dealing with in this moment is profound: a race between offense and defense. Between the proliferation of dark biology, where deadly pathogens are engineered in secret, and the promise of a new era of collective global health.

Every infectious disease outbreak begins with a handful of cases. Public health wins by learning about an outbreak before it spreads wide, before hospitals fill and a crisis starts to spiral out of control. As transmission rates explode, options shrink. One of AI’s greatest values is its ability to compress the timeline between outbreak and detection. Speed can mean the difference between containing an outbreak and confronting an epidemic, or another global pandemic.

The World Health Organization (WHO) now uses AI to track the spread of infectious disease. At the WHO’s Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, in Berlin, Germany, computational systems leverage artificial intelligence and pathogenic surveillance to track and monitor infectious disease outbreaks around the world. At the center of this new way forward sits a computer-based system called Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources, or Eios (“EE-oss”), which acts as a giant filter for the world’s minute-by-minute health information.

For decades, traditional epidemic intelligence has relied on official case counts. But data from hospitals, labs, research groups and other formal reporting systems takes days or weeks to register and input into official databases. Eios leverages the colossal power of modern computing and social media to get a more immediate picture of a disease outbreak. Eios focuses on unofficial reports, citizen chatter, local news reports, social media posts and more. Proficient across multiple languages, Eios scans millions of websites, feeds and platforms, searching for outbreaks as they happen. It scrapes, filters and ranks information. The goal of Eios is to pull signal from noise.

AI is a force multiplier, changing the biological sciences every day. The real question is not whether AI can do catastrophic harm in the realm of biological sciences – it most certainly can – but whether public health officials can figure out how to deploy AI as a defensive tool faster than malicious actors deploy it as an offensive one.

The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. AI systems can already help researchers navigate enormous bodies of biological knowledge that once required years of specialized training. They can explain complex laboratory techniques, locate obscure scientific literature, troubleshoot technical problems and suggest experimental designs. None of these capabilities is inherently dangerous. Together, however, they lower the barrier to entering what was once a highly specialized field.

The greatest concern is that AIs can help humans create genuinely novel, or new, forms of biology. Scientists are already exploring these possibilities, from mirror-image life to organisms designed with capabilities that do not already exist in nature. Until recently, these possibilities were largely confined to theory or science fiction. Biology is unlike any other technology because what it produces can reproduce, spread across borders, mutate, and evolve on its own. A software bug crashes a computer. A biological mistake can become self-propagating. Once a living organism is released into the world, it cannot simply be switched off or recalled. That biological weapons are alive is what makes them fundamentally different from every other class of weapon, from the arrow to the ICBM.

The race has already begun. As I cover in my forthcoming book Biological War, and this recent New York Times article outlines, biological weapons have an extremely low barrier to entry. Unlike nuclear weapons, which require tightly controlled fissile material and complex delivery systems, biological weapons can be built with widely available laboratory tools, aided by increasingly powerful AI systems.

The technology to engineer life is advancing faster than the existing laws, treaties and safeguards meant to govern it. This widening gap is where existential danger lives. The point is pressure, not panic. We need to develop AI systems to strengthen public health, accelerate disease detection and help build biological defenses as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design. Because once biology outruns our ability to contain it, there is no recalling what has already been unleashed upon the world.

Annie Jacobsen is the author of Biological War, to be published on 28 July by Dutton. She also wrote the Pulitzer prize–finalist in history The Pentagon’s Brain and the New York Times bestsellers Nuclear War, Area 51 and Operation Paperclip

fullText:
Research shows AI accounts are gaining millions of views on TikTok by spreading dubious health advice

Misleading health claims online pose a “huge danger to public safety”, experts have warned, after research has shown that AI-generated doctors are gaining millions of views on TikTok by spreading dubious health advice.

The British Medical Association council deputy chair, Dr Emma Runswick, flagged the risks posed by AI accounts that “peddle medical myths and promote so-called miracle cures”.

“Platforms like TikTok must do more to stop the rise of dangerous fake medical advice … otherwise, it is the public who could be paying the price with their health and perhaps even their lives,” she added.

AI-generated physicians were found to have spread disproven myths about cancer, including that microwaving food in plastic, using deodorants and sleeping next to your phone could all cause cancer – all claims which have been refuted by Cancer Research UK.

The research was published this month by Hallam, a digital marketing agency. It follows warnings by the NHS that health misinformation on social media was a “real threat to public health”.

The research found that AI-generated content appeared in 40% of top health-related TikTok videos, with most posted by a growing number of deepfake influencer accounts designed to resemble real doctors. For some specific search terms, such as “health tips”, 84% of videos were classed as AI-generated or AI-assisted content.

According to Hallam, top AI-generated doctor and health videos in their search received an average of 2.5m views. TikTok took down examples of the videos that were sent to the platform by the Guardian.

The accounts also promoted bizarre remedies for various health problems, including Coca-Cola mixed with onion as a pain-relief remedy and a fake product called “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” as an anti-ageing solution.

One avatar claimed he had recommended “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” to his patients for years, and that it could combat “hair loss, skin weakening, brittle nails and joint pain” by helping the body produce “anti-ageing molecules naturally”. The Guardian could not find evidence of “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” products online.

In response to the findings, Prof Frankie Swords, the national medical director at NHS England, said it was concerning to see a rise in online medical misinformation. “Many clinicians are reporting an increasing number of patients who feel worried and confused due to false advice that has been made solely for clicks,” she added.

Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, the president of the Royal College of GPs, said she was also concerned by the research, adding that misleading AI content carried a “real risk” of harm.

Hallam analysed 1,198 videos, selecting the top 50 videos across a series of search terms including “health tips” and “doctor advice”. It also looked for general “life-impacting” advice on issues such as personal finance and education.

Alex Ruani, health misinformation researcher at UCL, said the rise of AI doctor videos represented a “frightening amount of exposure to fake medical content”.

“We’re looking at industrialised exploitation of trust,” she added.

Last year, a poll conducted by Savanta on 3,575 men and 3,832 women aged 18 and above in England on behalf of patient champion Healthwatch England found that about one in five people were using social media for health information.

William Pett, interim director of policy and public affairs at Healthwatch England, said: “Without the skills to distinguish reliable information from commercial hype or misinformation, [people] risk being misled in ways that can seriously affect their health.”

A TikTok spokesperson said: “These findings from a marketing agency with commercial interests are not an accurate reflection of our platform.”

“The facts are that we remove harmful health misinformation, including when it’s AI-generated, we partner with the World Health Organization and the NHS on providing reliable health information in-app, and we continually invest in AI literacy resources and labelling technologies.”

title: They thought they'd be retiring. Instead, they're grandparenting full time.
description: Vicki and Sal Parisella are among the many US grandparents sacrificing retirement and health to raise grandchildren and keep them out of foster care.
fullText:
It's not the way they thought they'd be spending their older years: getting two tweens ready for school and scraping together meals from food banks.

At the crack of dawn one Tuesday morning, 59-year-old Vicki Parisella bangs on her granddaughters' bedroom doors. Silence from Myaliissa's room; a whine from Tatiana's. Minutes later, Tatiana drags her backpack into the living room.

"Your shirt's on backward," Vicki tells the 11-year-old.

As if Vicki flipped an on-switch, Tatiana zooms around the living room while Vicki's husband, Sal, packs their lunches. Vicki braids Tatiana's hair and helps her put on her shoes as Myaliissa, 13, gets dressed. By 7:20, Vicki already has a headache.

Vicki and Sal, 76, are part of a growing population of 1.1 million US grandparents 60 and older who have returned to parenting roles when they expected to be retiring.

Business Insider has spoken to more than 50 grandparents in this position in recent months. They said they've taken up parenting duties because of a child's death, drug use, or health issues. They all said they would make the decision to raise their grandchildren again in a heartbeat, though with few resources, most agreed that every day brought new financial and emotional challenges.

Noah Sheidlower spoke with Vicki and Sal Parisella over the course of six months to learn how raising two of their granddaughters in Lakeland, Florida, has changed their lives. He visited them for two days and reviewed financial, court, and medical records for this story. If you would like to share your story about grandparenting in America, fill out this quick form, and 

The new reality of being a grandparent

I'm 63 and raising four of my grandchildren. I haven't once thought about retiring.

I'm 73 and raising 3 great-grandchildren. Money is tight — I had to unretire to support my family.

Like many of the grandparents who spoke to Business Insider, Vicki and Sal rarely have enough money to make it through the month. Vicki, who's the sole breadwinner due to Sal's kidney condition, overdrew her bank account paying rent earlier this year. The family gets most of its meals from food banks. In July, they got an eviction notice they're disputing.

But all that can wait for later. For now, Vicki has to get the kids to school.

"We're going to be late. Run to the car," Vicki shouts.

Tatiana sprints, her lunchbox flopping by her side. Myaliissa follows, not saying a word.

After dropping the girls at school, Vicki lights a cigarette. She calls Sal as she winds through traffic in her 2023 Toyota Camry on the way to her accounts payable job.

"I caught the freaking train," she tells Sal as she gets stuck at a crossing. She arrives at her desk with 30 seconds to spare. Crisis averted this time, she says, knowing full well the train could ruin her morning tomorrow.

Vicki can't afford to risk her job, which nets her $615 a week. Sal receives $1,435 monthly in Social Security. It's enough for the family to break even, unless something breaks or someone gets sick.

US Census data in 2024 showed that more than 3 million children lived in households with grandparents who had some responsibility for their care. To avoid the foster care system and give their grandchildren a shot at promising futures, some grandparents have sacrificed their financial security, retirements, social life, and physical and mental well-being.

"What's going to happen to them if I die, since I don't want them in foster care?" Rebecca Black, 63, said she frequently asks herself as a grandmother raising two grandsons in Texas. Black said she's been financially strained, but retired so she could be more present in their lives.

Madalyn Conchola, 62, said that her four granddaughters, ages 7 through 19, struggled after she adopted them. With few financial or community support resources, most of her $70,000 annual salary, plus a small state subsidy, goes toward raising them. Five years and lots of hard work later, she said her granddaughters have all been thriving in school.

"As time goes on, my age and my ability to work and earn money loom over me," said Conchola, in Arizona. "I'm looking for other ways to try to generate an income."

It's a concern that has plagued Vicki and Sal. They've had temporary custody of their granddaughters since their daughter Siobhan's relationship fell apart in 2017. The 36-year-old still sees the girls, but said she hasn't been able to get back on her feet to raise them full time.

"I do feel bad because of the burden of everything they have, but there's nothing really that I can do right now about it until I move closer," says Siobhan, who lives in Tampa.

That year, the family was evicted from their three-bedroom home in Lakeland because they couldn't afford the $1,143 rent. They moved to a Salvation Army shelter and were able to get by with assistance from her coworkers and Vicki's sister, Nicole Spottke.

"They're both incredibly patient. They get frustrated, as would anyone who's exhausted does, but the girls are raised really well," said Spottke, 55. "Vicki would like to be able to give them more financially, but truly, I wish she'd get it through her head that the time that she gives to the kids — that's so much more important."

After two years, they were able to rent a home with a small pool, enough room for the girls to run around, and a quiet space for Vicki to decompress. The house wasn't without its problems —mold, flooding, and broken appliances — but for five years, it did the job. Vicki said their lives slowly improved.

When that house sold two years ago, they saw a huge rent spike when securing their next home — to $2,075 monthly, leaving them with $725 less to spend on everything else — food, clothes for the girls, and gas. They often come up short. Their backyard is covered with weeds, their front lawn is uneven, and the house is old, but unable to find any other place in their budget, they renewed their lease.

"We know there are people worse off than us, but I need to vent because I'm frustrated," Vicki says in her dark living room. She keeps the lights off to save electricity.

As she drives to pick up the girls, Vicki pauses at a stoplight and lets out a sigh. Every minute and every dollar matters, she says. Still, she tries not to push her frustrations onto her granddaughters.

"If the girls were taken from us, I would lose it because I'd be worried constantly," Vicki says, crossing over two lanes of traffic.

Vicki and Sal have been unable to permanently adopt their grandchildren because their father hasn't signed over his rights. If they challenged him in court, lawyers told them it could prompt him to try to regain custody, and they could lose the girls

Other grandparents told Business Insider how they have struggled to secure permanent parental rights. Though policies vary by state, the parents must generally relinquish their parental rights first, or grandparents must prove that the parents are unable or unwilling to care for their child — often due to neglect, incarceration, or severe illness — while showing that granting custody is in the child's best interest.

The complicated legal process often leaves grandparents with little financial assistance while raising their grandchildren because they often don't qualify for the same benefits as foster parents. Business Insider spoke with some grandparents who spent as much as $70,000 to secure legal custody.

Carol Leonard, 65, decided not to go to court to get custody of her two teenage grandsons in Louisiana. She can't afford an attorney; the last one she spoke with requested $800 upfront. Because the father's parental rights have not been terminated, he would be able to petition the court to regain custody. Still, she's been able to enroll them in school and get them medical care.

Siobhan, the girls' mother, said she is willing to relinquish her parental rights. She said she calls Myaliissa and Tatiana frequently. She lives with her fiancé and works in retail. Siobhan also lost custody of her two other children, who live with her fiancé's parents.

"I of course know them, but I don't really know them," Siobhan says of her daughters. "I could name a few things that they like and what they're into, but I don't know everything."

Vicki and Sal still hope they'll be able to adopt the girls someday, though they know the road will be long and tiring. Would they change anything about the lengths they've taken to protect the girls? "No freaking way," Vicki says.

Running late to pick up the girls from school, Vicki hurls her purse over her shoulder and gives Sal a kiss. She gets into her car, which they bought in January after their previous one was repossessed. It's been years since she's gotten her nails done or gone to the dentist. She's upped her anxiety medications. They've discussed bankruptcy with their lawyer.

Myaliissa and Tatiana both attend private school because their grandparents wanted an education infused with Christian values. Tuition is covered by scholarships; uniforms cost an extra $300 a year for both girls. On a recent report card, Tatiana got five As — and a Krispy Kreme doughnut from the school for each. For years, Myaliissa was chatty and animated, but she's recently gone back into her shell.

Children who have lived through adverse experiences with their birth parents are at increased risk for physical, developmental, and behavioral challenges, said Carol Musil, who spent years studying grandparents who served as primary caregivers while at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio. Her research shows that applies to caregivers as well; grandmothers raising grandchildren often have worse physical health, depressive symptoms, and stress compared to other grandmothers.

Tatiana and Myaliissa have missed out on some staples of childhood, including summer camp and most after-school activities. Yvette Lovell, Myaliissa's godmother, who has taught both girls at school, says the Parisellas are "salt-of-the-earth kind of people" who don't have enough support. She's seen Vicki and Sal make tough sacrifices, including shielding them from family drama.

"I've been in education for almost 40 years, and I can count the number of grandparents who have taken on being the core for the grandchildren as they have," Lovell says.

Back home from school, as the night progresses, Tatiana becomes restless. She'd like to stay up an hour later, running around the house, tickling Vicki and Sal. She grabs the family's photo book and heads to her room. Myaliissa drags her blanket through the hallway to her room.

Tatiana grabs the book and looks through it as Vicki and Sal get her ready for bed. She sees snapshots of the family's trip to Disney World and the time when they all put their feet in the ocean at Cocoa Beach. Absent are photos of the times Vicki shielded the girls from flooding, the court documents that determined their futures, and the tough conversations the grandparents had about whether to buy milk or pay the electricity bill.

For now, all that matters is those genuine smiles on the last page, conveying joy that, if only for a day here and there, keeps them going.

"We want you to have that when we're not around anymore," Vicki tells her, reaching for a hug. "We want you to remember and say, 'Grandma and Grandpa took good care of me.'"
